newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Conrail strikes new deal with CSX.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Conrail strikes new deal with CSX.

text.p: Conrail Inc and CSX Corp said Friday they had reached agreement on a revised $10.3 billion merger deal that sets the stage for a final breakup of Conrail after a bitter takeover battle.
The revised deal would pay Conrail shareholders $115 per share cash within 90 days and let CSX and Norfolk Southern Corp negotiate a division of Conrail's assets.
Announcement of the deal came late in the evening and followed a Conrail board meeting.

It formalised the end of Conrail Chairman David LeVan's sometimes emotional struggle to keep intact the railroad that was formed by the federal government in 1976 from six bankrupt Northeastern railroads.

"Conrail's board and management would have preferred for the Conrail system to remain intact. However, under the circumstances as they developed, we have succeeded in negotiating the best possible transaction for all of Conrail's constituencies," LeVan said in a statement released late Friday.

Conrail had announced an $8.4 billion cash-and-stock merger with CSX in October. But Norfolk Southern, with deeper pockets, soon launched its own bid for Conrail, seeking to prevent Conrail's monoply on lucrative Northeastern U.S. rail routes from falling to a competitor.
In January, Conrail shareholders rejected an increased CSX offer that still fell short of Norfolk Southern's $115 per share, all-cash bid.

The resulting stalemate was not broken until Norfolk Southern approached CSX with a plan to divide Conrail. That plan, presented Feb. 24, was accepted by all parties as the basis for dividing Conrail, Norfolk Southern said Friday.

"Norfolk Southern is gratified that we will be able to fulfil our promise to deliver $115 in cash per share to Conrail shareholders. We are also pleased that the contemplated agreement with CSX will redraw the railroad map to preserve and enhance competition in the East and guarantee balanced competition between two strong companies," it said.
Norfolk Southern said its plan would allow for competition between the two surviving railroads "at and between most of the major ports and markets east of the Mississippi."
Norfolk Southern and CSX said they would now enter talks on completing a joint purchase of Conrail shares and other details.

Under the new deal, CSX is to revise an existing tender offer for Conrail to offer $115 per share cash for all outstanding shares. The expiration would be set for April 18, but could be extended by CSX to June 2, 1997, meaning shareholders would be paid within 90 days.
Stock acquired in the tender would be placed in a voting trust, pending federal regulatory approval of the deal.
Conrail said its revised deal with CSX was not conditioned on CSX and Norfolk Southern reaching agreement on dividing Conrail.

Conrail said it had received assurances by CSX that there would be a "substantial commitment to Pennsylvania," with a "major operating presence" in Philadelphia as well as work shops in Altoona and Hollidaysburg and a service centre in Pittsburgh.
Also, three Conrail directors would be invited to join CSX's board. CSX Chairman John Snow said in a statement Friday he was confident of the deal winning federal approval.
